Today’s Plan
Your next assignment needs all of this. Open your IDE now.
Plan before you code IPO-S and flowcharts — working the problem out before typing. 15 min
Conditionals if, if-else, nested if -else, and the operators that go inside them. 25 min
Using math and stopping earlysqrt, ceil, floor, and how to end a program when the input is bad. 15 min
Read the Python_03 assignment before you start it. There is a lot of arithmetic, and the planning we do today is what keeps it 
straight.

P A R T  O N E
Plan Before You Code
Working the problem out before you type a single line.
About 15 minutes

IPO-S: Four Questions to Ask First
Answer these before writing code, and the code almost writes itself.
I
Input
What does the program 
need from the user?
FOR TODAY’S PROBLEM
The numeric grade
P
Process
What has to happen to 
turn input into output?
FOR TODAY’S PROBLEM
Decide which letter 
it maps to
O
Output
What does the program 
give back?
FOR TODAY’S PROBLEM
The letter grade
S
Storage
What variables do you 
need along the way?
FOR TODAY’S PROBLEM
grade, letterGrade
Process is the hard one. The other three are usually obvious once you read the problem.

Today’s Problem, Written as IPO-S
A person inputs a numerical grade. The program outputs the 
matching letter grade.
A:  90 – 100
B:  80 – 89
C:  79 and below
Input
numerical grade
Output
the letter grade
Storage
grade, letterGrade
Process
if grade >= 90
letterGrade = A
if grade >= 80 and grade < 90
letterGrade = B
if grade < 80
letterGrade = C
This is not Python yet — it is the plan, written so a person can read it.

The Same Plan, as a Flowchart
A picture of the decisions. Each shape means something specific.
Start
input grade
grade >= 90 ?
grade >= 80 ?
letterGrade = "C"
output letterGrade
End
No
No
Yes
letterGrade = "A"
Yes
letterGrade = "B"
What each shape means
Start or End
Input or output
A decision — two ways out
Something the program does
Notice there is one way in and one way out of 
the whole chart. Every path reaches End.

P A R T  T W O
Conditionals
Making the program choose between different paths.
About 25 minutes

The Operators You Need
These go inside the condition — the part between if and the colon.
Relational — compare two values
> greater than
>= greater than or equal to
< less than
<= less than or equal to
== equal to (two signs!)
!= not equal to
Boolean — join two conditions
and True only when BOTH sides are true
grade >= 80 and grade < 90
or True when EITHER side is true
day == 6 or day == 0
Each side of and must be a complete comparison.
80 <= grade and grade < 90   works
80 <= grade and < 90         does not

Program 1: Three Separate ifs
The direct translation of the IPO-S process block.
# Recitation problem 1
grade = int(input("Enter the integer numeric grade: "))
if grade >= 90:
letterGrade = "A"
if grade >= 80 and grade < 90:
letterGrade = "B"
if grade < 80:
letterGrade = "C"
print("Your letter grade is", letterGrade)
Sample runs
grade 95  ->  A
grade 85  ->  B
grade 72  ->  C
Watch the middle one
It needs and, because B is a range with a 
floor and a ceiling. Without the second half, 
a 95 would be relabeled B.
All three conditions are checked on every single run, even after the answer is 
known.

Program 2: Nested if-else
Same answers, different structure. Build this one line by line from Program 1.
# Recitation problem 2
grade = int(input("Enter the integer numeric grade: "))
if grade >= 90:
letterGrade = "A"
else:
if grade >= 80:
letterGrade = "B"
else:
letterGrade = "C"
print("Your letter grade is", letterGrade)
else means everything else
Reaching else already tells you grade < 90. You 
never have to test it again.
The and disappears
Inside that else, grade >= 80 is enough to mean 
80–89.
Indentation is the structure
The inner if-else is indented because it lives 
inside the outer else.
Both programs give identical answers for every grade. Try 95, 85 and 72 in each.

Which One Does Less Work?
Same answers — so compare them by counting how many comparisons each one makes.
Grade entered Letter Program 1 Program 2
95 A 4 comparisons 1 comparison
85 B 4 comparisons 2 comparisons
72 C 4 comparisons 2 comparisons
Where Program 1’s four comparisons come from
grade >= 90
grade >= 80 and grade < 90
grade < 80
→   1
→   2
→   1
Four comparisons on every run, whatever the grade is.
Why this matters
Four comparisons instead of one is 
invisible on a single grade. Run it over a 
million records and the difference is real.
Two correct programs are not always 
equally good. That judgment is a large 
part of computer science.

The Trap: A Gap in Y our Conditions
One wrong symbol and some inputs match nothing at all.
if grade > 90:          # should be >=
letterGrade = "A"
if grade >= 80 and grade < 90:
letterGrade = "B"
if grade < 80:
letterGrade = "C"
print("Your letter grade is", letterGrade)
Enter 90 and Python stops with:
NameError: name 'letterGrade' is not defined
What happened
90 is not greater than 90, so the first if 
fails. It is not below 90 either, so the 
second fails. And it is not under 80. No 
branch runs, letterGrade is never created, 
and print has nothing to show.
How to avoid it
Test the boundaries: 90, 89, 80, 79. Those 
four values catch almost every mistake of 
this kind.
Program 2 cannot have this problem — an else always catches whatever the if did not.

P A R T  T H R E E
Using math and Stopping 
Early
Square roots, rounding, and refusing bad input.
About 15 minutes

import math and Pythagoras
c² = a² + b², and the one line people forget.
import math
aStr = input("Enter value for a: ")
a = float(aStr)
bStr = input("Enter value for b: ")
b = float(bStr)
c = math.sqrt(a**2 + b**2)
print("c =", c)
With a = 3 and b = 4
c = 5.0
Leave out import math
and the program stops dead:
NameError: name 'math'
is not defined
Two things to notice
** is “to the power of”, so a**2 is a squared.
float, not int — lengths can have decimals.

ceil and floor, in Interactive Mode
Type one line, get one answer. The fastest way to check what a function does.
>>> import math
>>> math.ceil(4.2)
5
>>> math.floor(4.9)
4
Interactive mode
The >>> prompt runs one line at a time and prints the result 
immediately — no file, no Run button. Use it whenever you are unsure 
what something does.
All three rounders, side by side
Value ceil floor round
4.2 5 4 4
4.5 5 4 4
4.9 5 4 5
ceil always goes up and floor always goes down, whatever 
the decimal is. round goes to the nearest — and it sends a 
tie like 4.5 to the even number , so round(4.5) is 4, not 5.

Stopping a Program Early
If the input makes no sense, say so and stop — do not calculate with it.
aStr = input("Enter a positive value for a: " )
a = float(aStr)
if a <= 0:
print("Input error")
quit()
a = 5 Continues to the rest of the program
a = -2 Input error   →  program ends here
Guard your input
A negative length, a zero divisor, a grade 
of 500 — none of these should flow into 
your calculation. Check them first.
Both lines must be indented under the if, or 
the program quits every time — even on 
good input.

Before You Start the Assignment
Write the IPO-S first On paper, before any typing. Input, Process, Output, Storage.
Cast every input input() gives text. int() or float() it before any arithmetic.
Choose if-else over stacked ifs Fewer comparisons, and no gap for a value to fall through.
Test the boundaries Not just a middle value — the exact numbers where the answer changes.
import math before you use it sqrt, ceil and floor all need it.
